Review Title: Not just the best comic book based movie, but best movie of the year
Review: I saw the movie a couple of hours ago and I am blown away. It was spectacular, I'm seeing it again in a couple of days. This movie surpassed every other comic book based film-including the first Batman-in overall depth, character development, plot complexity, and yes, acting. Nolan did the near impossible, he took a man running around fighting bad guys in a bat suit-one who's face looks like a clown-and created a modern crime drama-a realistic interpretation of an unrealistic concept. It was gritty and simply delicious.This movie surpasses the original batman not because of it's modern day action, or special effects, but because of it's sound story and-of course-of ledger's brilliant acting. There are several plot developments and twists that had me bouncing out of my seat. Burton's Batman was very good, it set the bar, and that bar has remained unsurpassed until TDK. Burton's Batman was set in a comic like world, it felt detached from Our concept of reality-but of course, this is what Burton intends to do. It's his mind literally bleeding on film. This is what makes his movies so entertaining, his ability to bring his own private images to on screen in stunning clarity; his originality is stupendous. I say all this because I want ya'll to know How much I love Burton, but that doesn't change the fact that this movie is much better than it. This movie felt like it could actually happen today. The terroristic theme of the film was great.Now, on to Ledger. His performance was better than Jacks in every way possible. The little facial reactions; the smacking of lips; the hand movements; the walk; acting at it's best. Jack's Joker was funny, Heath's was terrifying, he never gave an inch. At all times he was completely insane. It's a shame he passed, what a great performance his was. Maggie was excellent as Racheal, the depth of her character was bright at all times. Bale was superb, he is truly Batman. Morgan's performance was also fantastic, as well was Cain's. I gave this movie a 9/10 only because it had minor flaws; these flaws may even be nick picking, but in my head they exist. I didn't care that much for Two Face's distorted area of his face. I don't really know why, but It didn't have that stamp of authenticity to it, but this didn't detract from the greatness of the movie. Also, Bale's voice as batman sounded a bit overdone-almost like a grunt. I didn't care for this either. Other than that this movie lived up to the hype and in ways surpassed it.Enjoy the film!!

The Dark Knight is to the superhero film what The Godfather is to the gangster movie. Nolan's filmmaking always teaches us to question the truth--to question what we know to be true, and the Dark Knight is no exception to the Nolan rule. A blistering deconstruction of the superhero genre--the most popular genre of the decade--The Dark Knight questions how far a hero should go in pursuit of a villain. The film responds to the problems caused by GW Bush's war on terror by offering us one of the most compelling and terrifying characters in modern cinema: Heath Ledger's version of The Joker. Like Anthony Hopkins' Hannibal Lecter or Anthony Perkins' Norman Bates, Ledger's Joker is so frighteningly fascinating and magnetic that I faced a conundrum when first watched the film: I couldn't wait for him to come on screen again--and i was cringing with horror every time he did. The film is visceral, accomplished, and spectacular. Bale's Batman is a study in contradictions, and in that way, he reflects his historical moment--the moment of the war on terror--very effectively.

Three years after virtuoso thriller director Christopher Nolan resurrected one of cinema's great conflicted heroes, he returns with a dark and brooding vision of corruption more cynical than anything in Wilder or Welles. In a genre-transcending meditation on the nature of evil and it's prevalence in society, Nolan, and his terrific cast led by Christian Bale and the late Heath Ledger, has crafted something more than a comic book film, more than a crime chronicle; he has produced for our viewing pleasure a great modern tragedy.Reprising his role as the Caped Crusader is the irreplaceable Bale, estranged from his namesake corporation and famed mansion, still stalking the night. The rising prominence of lion-hearted district attorney Harvey Dent (Aaron Eckhart) has eased his load as Gotham's silent guardian, promising a blindingly bright future as the city's infamous crime organizations are ravaged by a seemingly harmless radar-blip villain known only as the 'Joker.' This infectiously charismatic, godless menace is portrayed by Heath Ledger, and it is the most viscous, hauntingly villainous performance I have yet seen on screen. Unmotivated by money, sex or power, the Joker simply wants to "watch the world burn." He is Mahmoud Ahmadinejad in a green vest, a wholly original caricature of evil more fully realized than any so-called 'bad guy' to grace the screen in years. The air-tight tension and frenzied, yet occasionally contemplative pacing of Nolan"s 152- minute opus allows for little time to think. Nolan ensures that his audience reacts instinctually to the drama without allowing time for analysis. It is a whirlwind of a cinematic experience that intends for the audience to appreciate every moment of the film; in other words, watch now, digest later. The film traverses nimbly from disaster to death, not bothering to wait for us to catch up.Unlike lauded crime films such as "Heat," "The Departed," and "The Untouchables," which it has on many occasions been compared to, "The Dark Knight" has ideals, revolutionary, even controversial ideals that separate it from even the most ambitious comic book fare. Nolan, the film's composer, imagines an irreparably corrupt society without hope; absence of innocence and honesty as elements of the human condition; and the banishment of heroes as the only means judicial satisfaction in world too afraid to face itself. And in these criminal parables lies a message that is unavoidably political. Can one help but compare Harvey Dent, the 'white knight' with the potential to rid a crime-ridden city of violence once and for all, to Barack Obama, the youthful, saving grace of American politics primed to cleanse the White House of a most unforgettable reign? It is in these ideals that "The Dark Knight" transcends it's genre, evolving from a slab top-notch entertainment to an indisputable masterpiece.Bale is great as ever, as are Gary Oldman in a significantly beefier role as Lieutenant James Gordon and Michael Caine as the wise old fountain of wisdom. Eckhart is sensational as Harvey Dent in a multi-faceted performance that leaves Tommy Lee Jones' incarnation of Two-Face in the dust. And then there's Heath Ledger, in perhaps the greatest swan song in the lore of cinema. Indeed, his Joker will undoubtedly come to be known as one of the greatest villains in film history. That disorienting, surreal powdery-rouge makeup blended with Ledger's inimitable affect paint a portrait of a villain unlike anything that I myself have ever seen, a hollow soul that we try desperately to identify with until the film's final frame. Ledger virtually owns the film from it's commencement to it's credits; by film's end he is a larger-than-life persona amplified one thousand times by the tragedy millions have yet to recover from. Watching Ledger, one can't help but wonder what could have been, yet we can take comfort in the fact that his last performance was the role of a lifetime.Arguably Nolan's greatest achievement to date, "The Dark Knight" will not merely settle for being the glory of being one of the greatest comic book adaptations. It's an overwhelming work of art with the gravitas of a Greek tragedy and the technical prowess of one of the medium's great modern works. Quite simply, it's one of the greatest movies of our time.

Christopher Nolan's second bundle of joy "The Dark Knight" EXCEEDED all of my expectations!!! With the success of 2005's reboot of the Batman franchise, they took what was already established and expanded it, amped it up, and gave a deeper, darker and brooding story that is more gripping and the suspense is likely to catch you of guard several times throughout. Christian Bale delves more deeper into Batman, sworn to fight evil and injustice, though also quite reluctant and uncertain if his crusade can ever end and cleanse his inner turmoil from his fractured soul due to the murder of his beloved parents. But with the help of his trusted butler/ally Alfred (played superbly by Michael Cane) grounds him, gives him moral support, and keeps him in check. But the real star of the show is Heath Ledger as Batman's most deadly enemy, The Joker. I can HONESTLY tell you that: as good as Jack Nicholson was in Batman'89 he is CHILD'S PLAY compared to this Joker. He is sadistic, psychotic, and downright SCARIER and PSYCHOLOGICALLY disturbing than the previous incarnation of The Clown Prince of Crime and Ledger gives it his all to do him justice. Along with the original cast comes some fresh faces such as Aaron Eckhart, Maggie Gyllenhaal and more. I must say though I liked Katie Holmes, Gyllenhaal gives a much better performance and is a far cry from the "damsel-in-distress" stereotype (though there's a little of it, THANKFULLY) that's common in films. Bale and Gyllenhall have MUCH better chemistry this time around more so than Holmes. Even better, the fight sequences are vastly improved and feature more brutal and bone crushing combat than "Begins" in addition to new technology at Batman's disposal. Also worth mentioning is screenwriter Jonathan Nolan, who gives the film an added frosting to an already delicious cake. Simply put, The Dark Knight is totally more bad ass than "Begins." The action is great, and the plot is more deeper and engrossing. I applaud Christopher Nolan, Christian Bale, and especially Heath Ledger (who sadly passed away earlier this year) and all those aboard for believing in Mr. Nolan's talents for this second installment. Although some may feel a bit of melancholy over Ledger's death, but as a final note I will say this sincerely from my heart: Remember Heath Ledger and honor him in your minds and hearts not only for his performances, but as a human being and father to his daughter Matilda Ledger. May we issue him best wishes for his family and friends and his daughter for years to come. Remember . . . Honor him not only for this role and past roles, but as an incredible individual and talented actor. Rest in peace. Heath Ledger: 4/4/1979-1/22/2008.

But after Batman does his thing, the film bends down to unnecessary philosophy over good and evil, you'll see what I mean.All in all, a very good effort by Christopher Nolan, but it could have been more intense and sleek, without the unnecessary philosophy in the end. It's almost like he is playing Batman all the time, just without the mask.What really makes this movie a good movie is not the acting, or even the story. They are put together so well that you really feel that you are in Gotham watching the story unfold.In summary, definitely see this movie, but keep in mind the evil quotient is a bit forcefully high, and the acting and story do not feel believable, except Two Face.

There are several aspects about the Dark Knight that make it stand apart from other superhero films, but the most iconic feature of the movie is Heath Ledger's portrayal of the Joker. Though not the first to take up the mantle of the Batman's most infamous super-villain, Heath Ledger's take placed the character in a considerably darker and more mature light. The more traditional versions of the Joker offered audiences a dastardly, unpredictable clown with a white paint-plastered face, and while Heath Ledger's Joker is indeed unpredictable, he is definitely no clown. In full costume Ledger stands with a hunched posture in a purple suit, a face covered in white makeup, and an unnerving red smile painted across his lips and cheeks. The overall image is haunting, but what truly sets this act apart is in the monologues of Ledger's Joker. His words are not those of a wise- cracking psychopath, but those of precise and dangerous serial killer. "I'll show you," Ledger tells co-star Christian Bale (the Batman) in one scene. "When the chips are down, these civilized people...they'll eat each other." The Dark Knight may very well be the greatest superhero movie of all time, and it's all because of the talents of Heath Ledger. He's not crazy. He's just ahead of the curve.

Now get that mind out of the gutter. This is my "The Dark Knight" official review. No Spoilers, no worries.I just want to say that right off the bat (no pun intended) Nolan is a genius. Technically he stole my idea...but I'm okay with it. He didn't have opening credits....I thought of that idea when I first started getting into film four years ago. So he got the nod from me quickly.The music was amazing. Why? Because if you were to listen to the first two pieces of the film without watching the film, or know where it was from, you would be creeped out or just drop your jaw. Not to mention it is so different from the score of Batman Begins.The writing for the film was impeccable. Well done by both the Nolan brothers. I did hear a couple complaints about the dialogue being some-what "unconventional." However when have you ever watched a good film with anything but it. Excluding stupid comedies. I think this was the most I have ever really read into what people were saying during any film I've seen.The shots are amazing. Because all of the stunts are real and they don't use much CGI it almost makes you nervous for the actors, but it made it that much more enjoyable. Which in turn made the shots indescribable.The directing was immaculate. I would expect nothing less from Nolan. I can't really put into words what he has done for the Batman World. All I can say is: In Nolan We Trust.Now the acting. Bale was as good as he was in Begins, if not better. For those of you that discussed Begins with me, know the only problem I had was his voice under the cowl. In this it didn't bother me as much. Michael Caine, disappointingly was not as present as he was in Begins, but he still had the British charm, and had some key lines that really hit me. Morgan Freeman played a much bigger role in this film. And I enjoyed him more in TDK. And it has left me intrigued to see what direction they take his character in the next one. Maggie Gyllenhaal! What a surprise she was. Wayyyy better than Katie Holmes. And I think she definitely added some sex appeal to the film. Aaron Eckhart, was very very convincing being Harvey Dent. I was a little concerned about how well the Bruce/Harvey story would go because in the comics they were good friends. They developed that well, and a very friendly rivalry also went on between them. But how friendly was it really? Now to the guy. The one name that deserves his own paragraph. Heath. Before I write about his performance, I just want to say. I had my doubts. I kind of was unsure about an Oscar nod. The Oscar system is a tough one to infiltrate in the acting world. However, after seeing this, in my mind he was hands down the best villain I have ever had the enjoyment of watching. In some instances, I couldn't breathe while watching what he was going to do next. It is definitely Oscar worthy. The biggest thing that did it for me was his voice. If you have ever heard what Heath really sounded like, and what he sounds like in all of his movies, but haven't seen the movie, see it. It is worth the 10.25 or 14.50 for the voice alone. Oddly comical, convincingly evil and just a creepy son of a bitch. Well done Heath.As for the movie as a whole, I have never given a 5/5 or a 10/10 in any movie ever. I always find a problem or an issue. Even in The Prestige, which was the closest to my favorite movie as you are going to get, had issues with me. But this movie is the only, and probably will always be the only, film I will give a 10/10 score. So, that being said, well done to everyone involved. And enjoy making 200 million + this weekend.

Review Title: Superb Batman movie but it suffers from an identity crisis
Review: My anticipations for 'The Dark Knight' were great. First of I have to say overall I'm not disappointed. The movie definitely earns its praise as one of the best (if not the best) movie of 2008 so far. I can also see where other people's claims like "best Batman movie" and "best comic movie of all time" are coming from. Although for me, it doesn't entirely feel that way. Let me explain my view.My major complaint concerns the 'character' of this movie. This movie made me question what kind of 'character' the director wanted to give to 'The Dark Knight'. It made me ask myself if this movie works, in the first place, as the kind of movie it's supposed to be (a comic book translation to the screen). The main problem with 'The Dark Knight' is that it doesn't really seem to know what kind of movie it wants to be and what kind of impressions and emotions it wants to carry over on the audience. Because what is this movie really when you think about it? It's a movie translation from a comic book. But aside from the necessary 'comical' appearance of characters and elements in the movie (Batman and all his gadgetry, the Joker, Two-Face) the movie doesn't seem to present itself as a comic movie whatsoever. Its main shortcome is that it doesn't quite succeed in embodying the spirit of a comic book.While it was already apparent in 'Batman Begins' that Christopher Nolan wants to give a Batman movie a more realistic and more adult touch, he pushes this even further with 'The Dark Knight'. 'The Dark Knight' tries very hard to be something more (or something else?) than just a mere Batman movie. In fact, it could be considered a psychological thriller/mafia and crime movie/action movie/serial killer or horror movie, all combined in one film. But what is essentially the problem here? It needs to remain a Batman movie. It needs to maintain its identity as a comic book movie. If that doesn't happen, then what's the point in making one? If you want to make it too real, you could just as well completely remove all comic elements from it and make a realistic crime thriller with real-life characters and situations.Nolan gives the impression that he doesn't seem to realize this. Of course, we all know that probably isn't true, and he just wants to show the darker and more adult side of the Batman comics in his movies. There is nothing wrong with that. But reaching this goal by pushing the amount of realism in your movies to the very possible extremes is probably not the best way to achieve this and to convey the message. Nolan made Batman as realistic as he could with the result being a movie that doesn't quite know what it wants to be. Is it meant to be a comic book movie or a psychological crime thriller? Is it meant for adults or for kids? Is it fantastic or realistic? 'The Dark Knight' has a PG-13 rating meaning that kids will also be able (and are probably willing) to see this new Batman movie. However, they probably won't get much enjoyment out of it. The dark and depressing tone, the violence, the complex plot and dialogues and all other 'adult' elements will put them off. But at the same time, although making an adult and realistic Batman movie, Nolan clearly wanted this movie to be bound to certain limits. For instance, the movie never really gets graphic in showing violence, blood or other disturbing images. This makes the movie, in some way, not convincing enough as being an entirely dark and adult movie. If you want to make an adult Batman, why not go all the way? Adult comic book translations have been made effectively before. Take Sin City. That movie was a comic book movie at heart. It captured the spirit of the comic completely and at the same time had a very convincing adult character. It was far from realistic but it didn't have to be. It also didn't pretend to be something other than an adult comic book movie.Anyway, enough criticizing, you get the main idea of my complaint, and by doing this I might be giving the impression that I didn't like this movie, which obviously (see the 8 star rating), isn't the case. I actually liked it very much, in spite of the movie's apparent identity crisis. Obviously I was blown away by Heath Ledger's Joker, but the overall acting of the entire cast was actually very good (not a big fan of Bale's Batman voice though). Screenplay, editing and all that was great too. The movie also had a great story progression and a very comfortable and effective way of making the progress of the story flow. It didn't make the film seem as lengthy as it was at all. There were some scenes that were actually quite excellent and really well thought out. The words "pencil trick", "police questioning", "hospital scene" and "social experiment" should make a bell ring for those people who've already seen it. In the end, I really wasn't disappointed at all. I was simply questioning some of the ideas behind the movie. And that sorta stopped me from giving it a higher score, because a perfect movie shouldn't make me question myself if perhaps it couldn't have been handled more effectively to stay true to the real intentions and ideas behind it. That is all. Thanks for reading this.

Review Title: Not enough can be said about this movie.
Review: The Dark Knight lives up to the hype, and far surpasses it. I saw this movie late, over a week after it came out. First of all, disregard this movie as a "superhero" "comic book" movie, because it is much more. The psychology of the joker is truly terrifying, and fully realistic. I found myself wondering exactly how much of an effect playing this character had on Heath Ledger's own psyche, as his performance is so well done that you come to understand that such acting can only be done by becoming the character, as opposed to just "acting." Jack Nicholson is a great actor, but this joker is less cartoonish, mor philosophical in a terrifying sense, and much darker.As a whole, the movie explores some serious sociological themes, as humans are used as pawns acting against one another, provoked by suspicion and paranoia. The exploration of power in its many forms is fully explored in the film, and almost leaves one sick in how accurately it portrays the true nature of the human race, and how we often fight against ourselves in order to do what we know is right.In essence, this film is not only dark and scary because of camera lighting and film-making tricks, but because it explores themes and issues that ring very true to the modern day world, but that we either do not see or choose to ignore.On a closer film orientated standpoint, all of the performances given are brilliant, and I can honestly say, without bias pertaining to Heath Ledger's death, that the joker is possibly the most terrifying villain ever put on screen. The film is very action oriented, and despite its running of 2 1/2 hours, the film does not ever feel long. There are enough plot twists to keep the viewer off balance, and the ending is perfect.Great film, great directing, great acting, and especially, great writing. Congratulations to the Nolan brothers and David S. Goyer on bringing the public a movie that is truly worth watching.

The Dark Knight is a 2008 superhero film directed, co-produced, and co-written by Christopher Nolan. Featuring the DC Comics character Batman, the film is the second part of Nolan's The Dark Knight Trilogy and a sequel to 2005's Batman Begins, starring an ensemble cast including Christian Bale, Michael Caine, Heath Ledger, Gary Oldman, Aaron Eckhart, Maggie Gyllenhaal and Morgan Freeman. In the film, Bruce Wayne/Batman (Bale), James Gordon (Oldman) and Harvey Dent (Eckhart) form an alliance to dismantle organized crime in Gotham City, but are menaced by a criminal mastermind known as the Joker (Ledger) who seeks to undermine Batman's influence and create chaos.Nolan's inspiration for the film was the Joker's comic book debut in 1940, the 1988 graphic novel The Killing Joke, and the 1996 series The Long Halloween, which retold Two-Face's origin. The nickname "the Dark Knight" was first applied to Batman in Batman #1 (1940), in a story written by Bill Finger.[4][5] The Dark Knight was filmed primarily in Chicago, as well as in several other locations in the United States, the United Kingdom, and Hong Kong. Nolan used IMAX 70 mm film cameras to film some sequences, including the Joker's first appearance in the film. The film is dedicated to the memory of Ledger, who died on January 22, 2008, some months after the completed filming and six months before the film's release, from a toxic combination of prescription drugs, leading to intense attention from the press and movie-going public. Warner Bros. initially created a viral marketing campaign for The Dark Knight, developing promotional websites and trailers highlighting screenshots of Ledger as the Joker.A co-production of the United States and the United Kingdom, The Dark Knight was released on July 16, 2008 in Australia, on July 18, 2008, in North America, and on July 25, 2008, in the United Kingdom. Considered by film critics to be one of the best films of the 2000s and one of the best superhero films ever,[6][7] the film received highly positive reviews and set numerous records during its theatrical run.[8] The Dark Knight appeared on more critics' top ten lists (287) than any other film of 2008 with the exception of WALL-E, and more critics (77) named The Dark Knight the best film of 2008 than any other film released that year.[9] With over $1 billion in revenue worldwide, it is the 29th-highest-grossing film of all time, unadjusted for inflation.[10] The film received eight Academy Award nominations; it won the award for Best Sound Editing and Ledger was posthumously awarded Best Supporting Actor.[11] The Dark Knight Rises, the final film in the trilogy, was released on July 20, 2012.

Review Title: A Spectacular Sequel and Tribute to a Lost Talent
Review: I just got back from seeing this movie, and in a word: Marvelous. Heath Ledger was even better than the hype. I found myself anxiously awaiting his next screen appearance. Morgan Freeman, Gary Oldman, and Michael Caine were all stellar in their respective roles, but I was pleasantly surprised by Aaron Eckhart's Harvey "Two-Face" Dent. Overall, he was very convincing and held his ground in a movie full of excellent performances.The action and fight sequences were all very well done, and I disagree with some of the statements that this didn't have enough of Batman kicking butt, because it certainly had plenty. It also had one of the coolest opening scenes in recent history, in my opinion. There were some new Bat-gadgets thrown in as well, which was good to see. The cinematography was absolutely spectacular. Some of the overhead and tracking shots were simply outstanding and helped to give the movie its grand scale.As for the downfalls, the movie is a tad long. While it never drags, I think they could have trimmed the fat. (Excluding any Joker scenes, of course.) Christian Bale's Batman voice got annoying a couple of times, but it doesn't really detract from the movie and he's so great besides that so I won't hold it against him. Maggie Gyllenhaal, while not as terrible as everyone said she was, definitely could have been better. My last complaint is that the ending, while great, didn't leave as much anticipation for the next movie (assuming there is one) as Batman Begins did. Overall...Rating: 9/10 - Certainly a must-see for any fan of Batman, and fans of movies for that matter.R.I.P. Heath Ledger

Review Title: The Dark Knight is Brought to Light
Review: The Dark Knight is the second movie of Christopher Nolan's Batman trilogy. It is the story of the ultimate comic book bad versus evil where Batman, played by Christian Bale, and The Joker, played by Heath Ledger, take their individual sides separately. The constantly moving camera angles that Nolan sets out to shoot, immerses the audience into the movie itself. It becomes known early on in the film that the Joker is a villain unlike no other that holds no rules or justice for anyone. Justice that Batman uses as his motives of his actions. Nolan's story writing is not just a sheet cake but multiple tiered cake, just as expected from his other films. It perfectly complements Jokers personality of a genius psycho villain. Another signature cinematic style used by Nolan in the Batman trilogy is the dark and gritty feel of the camera. This kind of filtration deserves seriousness and deeper thoughts, a statement to show the world that this is no child-friendly superhero movie but a story that has a real world presence. All of the stylistic film noir that Christopher Nolan uses constantly compliments one another to bring for the best superhero movie and possibly one of the best movie stories.

Review Title: The Dark Knight is a good film that will be forgotten eventually
Review: The Dark Knight is a good action movie that features tightly crafted action sequences and it boasts a decent story to tie it all together. Sadly though the story is still drawn out like all comic book movies. The acting also is very bland with only Heath Ledger, Morgan Freeman, and Michael Caine performing well.The direction is solid and Nolan has learned from his mistakes in Batman Begins. To say the least though, the film needed a better editor as the film kind of drags on past it's expiry date. For a movie this long it needed a really good story but it lacked it and the ending is terrible. Overall though it's a good film, just not one of the best of 2008. It'll be a fun movie to see for a night but the Dark Knight won't have you looking back on it as a classic.
